query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled surface fluorination treatment applied to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will trigger the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale (predominantly HfO2 and TiO2) during high‐temperature exposure, significantly reducing oxygen ingress without altering the bulk microstructure and baseline mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Spray-apply a dilute NaF-containing aqueous solution (or similar fluorinating agent) onto the alloy surface, followed by a short controlled isothermal oxidation treatment at 1000 °C in air.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 1000 °C (with a treatment duration on the order of a few hours up to 100 h as needed for scale formation) and testing at strain rates comparable to 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1; the intervention is applied only to the surface so that the intrinsic bulk ductility and high-temperature yield strength are maintained.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, dense, and adherent protective oxide layer (primarily HfO2 and TiO2) that acts as an effective diffusion barrier against oxygen.
generation.mechanism: Fluorine at the surface reacts to form volatile metal fluorides that preferentially promote the rapid formation of a protective oxide film during subsequent high-temperature exposure. This film limits oxygen penetration – similar to the fluorine effect observed in Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys – thereby preserving the alloy’s mechanical integrity during service.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated HfNbTaTiZr alloy will exhibit substantially reduced oxidation (lower weight gain during isothermal oxidation) while retaining its as-cast mechanical properties (similar ductility and yield strength) at high temperatures.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr readily oxidizes under high-temperature air exposure, leading to eventual degradation of mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be effective as long as the fluorination remains a surface-only modification that does not alter the bulk microstructure; the oxidation treatment must be optimized to form a protective but non-excessively thick and non-spalling scale. Excess fluorination or over-oxidation could lead to embrittlement, which would limit the validity of the intervention.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extrapolates the beneficial fluorination effect demonstrated in γ-TiAl alloys (as reported in PMC9030595, section 4 Conclusions and section 1 Introduction) to HfNbTaTiZr, whose specific oxide scale composition and long-term stability under cyclic mechanical loading remain to be confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples. Treat one set with the dilute NaF solution followed by a controlled isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C for a fixed duration. Keep the second set as untreated controls. Subject both sets to prolonged high-temperature exposure in air and perform mechanical testing (room temperature tensile and high-temperature yield strength measurements).
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analyses (SEM/TEM) and XRD to assess oxide scale phase, thickness, and adherence
Tensile tests to determine yield strength and ductility at room temperature and 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fluorine-treated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain and/or if they suffer any degradation in ductility or yield strength relative to the untreated controls, then the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In view of engineering applications, the convenient and inexpensive methods to introduce fluorine into large-sized γ-TiAl components have received extensive attention, such as dipping and spraying. For instance, the NH4F solution-impregnated γ-TiAl alloy could form a dense and continuous Al2O3 film and thus improve the anti-oxidation []. The surface of γ-TiAl alloys were immersed into the HF solution for long-term protection []. In order to meet the low-cost demands of industrial applications, the smart reintroduction of fluorine in the fluorine-treated γ-TiAl alloys system offers a highly attractive solution for engineering repairs, particularly in repairing surface protective oxide film on blades and turbine disks based on γ-TiAl alloys. In this work, the fluorine effect was applied for improving the high temperature oxidation resistance of the Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloy and its oxides. The fluorine-treated γ-TiAl alloy and its oxidized specimen with artificial defects were investigated by isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C. Furthermore, SEM and TEM characterizations revealed the evolution of the phase and microstructure of the oxidized specimens with artificial defects.

In this study, we executed a simple and effective strategy involving a two-step spraying and oxidation process to produce Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys with a dense Al2O3 film for application at high temperatures. The main results are as follows: (1)The oxidation resistance was significantly improved due to the formation of a protective Al2O3 film induced by the fluorine effect during isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C (6.03 mg/cm2 weight gain for the bare Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys, but 0.81 mg/cm2 for the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys).(2)The Ti diffused along the artificial microcracks, resulting in a quick growth of TiO2 in a short time (2 h), while a continuous Al2O3 film was generated underneath the oxide scale during further isothermal oxidation (100 h).(3)The Al2O3 particles between the alloy and continuous Al2O3 film were reflected in the γ-TiAl and α2-Ti3Al phases, which improved the adhesion of the oxide scale (fluorine-treated specimen had a deep yellow oxide scale on the surface without any exfoliation). These findings represent significant progress towards reducing the high temperature oxidation resistance of TiAl intermetallics by surface fluorine modification.
